title: Even If Hormuz Reopens, War-Risk Insurance Is Unlikely to Fall Quickly, Insurers Say, With Mines, Trapped Ships and Renewed-Hostility Risk
summary: Insurance Business (June 15, 2026) reports that war-risk premiums rose from about 0.1% to around 1% per S&P Global, that hundreds of ships remain stranded, and that insurers want evidence a US-Iran deal is holding before pricing normalises.
description:
A deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz does not mean war-risk insurance prices will return to normal quickly. That is the message of an Insurance Business report published on June 15, 2026, which draws on S&P Global, Howden Re, Pen Underwriting, Wood Mackenzie and Bloomberg. The report says that a US-Iran agreement may reopen the strait, that President Trump said it could reopen by Friday, and that oil prices fell, but that marine insurers are keeping their guard up. This article summarises that report, with a note on later developments. An earlier version of this article gave war-risk premiums of 3% to 8% of vessel value as an estimate from the same report. Those figures come from a different Insurance Business article published on June 28, which cites Marsh, and the June 15 report cites S&P Global figures of about 0.1% rising to around 1%. The two sets of figures are from different dates and sources, and are explained separately here.

What do the premium figures say? According to S&P Global, cited in the June 15 report, war-risk premiums rose from about 0.1% to around 1% of vessel value as hostilities escalated. The report's lead says premiums reached as much as 30 times pre-conflict levels. In the later June 28 report, the pre-conflict rate is given as about 0.25% of hull value, with a peak as high as 10% according to Dylan Saunders-Mortimer of Marsh, and current estimates of 3% to 8%, equal to $3 million to $8 million for one large tanker transit. These differences show that war-risk pricing is negotiated vessel by vessel and changes quickly, and that sources use different baselines. Readers should treat the numbers as indicative.

How has the market behaved? Howden Re described the hull war, cargo war and political violence markets as under extreme pressure. Insurers expanded their high-risk zones and scrutinised vessel movements more closely. Many used seven-day cancellation provisions, standard in war-risk policies, to withdraw cover and reissue it at higher rates. Simmonds of Pen Underwriting defended the practice as a way to keep capacity available, saying no single insurer is overexposed because capacity is shared. In plain terms, war-risk insurers can reprice every week, which is why prices can rise suddenly and fall more slowly.

What is holding back normalisation? Bloomberg reported uncertainty about potential mines, as well as electronic interference, navigation safety and the risk of renewed hostilities. Hundreds of vessels remain stranded on either side of the strait, waiting for clarity before resuming normal operations. Simmonds noted that the strait is about 21 miles wide at its narrowest point, which concentrates risk. The report does not mention naval or other escorts, though a separate article on this site describes how Berkshire Hathaway's Ajit Jain referred to US Navy escort assurances as part of the underwriting terms for a government-backed programme.

What are the wider effects? Wood Mackenzie said the closure removed more than 80 million tonnes a year of liquefied natural gas supply, roughly 20% of worldwide supply. That is why the strait matters to energy importers far from the Gulf. Higher insurance costs are passed on in freight rates and, ultimately, in prices, although safety concerns, not only insurance, also limit transits.

How long might it take? Simmonds said the market will want evidence that the agreement is holding and vessels can transit safely before pricing normalises, adding that it is not something that happens overnight. In the June 28 report, Neeraj Gupta of Policybazaar UAE said underwriters need two to four weeks of confirmed de-escalation before lower risk feeds into pricing, and that a full return to pre-conflict rates could take several months. That article also says a ceasefire signed earlier in June was undermined by renewed hostilities on June 27. Conditions have continued to change since, and readers should check current news for the latest status.

What does it mean for businesses and consumers? Importers, exporters and shipping lines should expect that cover remains expensive and subject to short-notice cancellation. They may seek to spread costs through contracts, use government-backed facilities where available, or reroute where feasible. For consumers, the effect is indirect, through the cost of fuel and goods. Insurers' willingness to return depends on the stability of the ceasefire and the physical safety of transits.

How does war-risk cover differ from ordinary marine insurance? Standard hull and cargo policies exclude war and related perils, which are covered separately under war-risk policies that can be cancelled at short notice and repriced for each voyage or zone. That is why a ship can have its normal insurance intact but still be unable to sail into a listed area without extra cover. Shipowners, charterers and lenders usually require cover to be in place before a vessel moves, so the availability and price of war-risk insurance can decide whether a voyage happens at all.

Why does a deal not fix it immediately? Underwriters price on the likelihood of attack, mine strikes and detention, and a signed agreement reduces that likelihood only if it holds. Until there is a track record of safe transits, insurers will keep zones and cancellation rights in place. That is a rational response to uncertainty, though it is frustrating for those waiting for costs to fall.

This article summarises press reports of a fast-moving situation and is not insurance, shipping or investment advice.
source_name: Insurance Business (S&P Global, Howden Re, Pen Underwriting, Wood Mackenzie, Bloomberg) and Khaleej Times
image_alt: Oil tanker in the Gulf as marine war-risk insurance premiums stay elevated near the Strait of Hormuz (illustrative)
key_points: S&P Global figures cited by Insurance Business show war-risk premiums rising from about 0.1% to around 1% of vessel value as hostilities escalated; other estimates in press coverage are higher.
Howden Re described hull war, cargo war and political violence markets as under 'extreme' pressure, and insurers expanded high-risk zones and scrutinised vessel movements more closely.
Many insurers used seven-day cancellation clauses to withdraw cover and reissue it at higher rates; Pen Underwriting's Simmonds says capacity is shared so no single insurer is overexposed.

Hundreds of vessels remain stranded on either side of the strait, which is about 21 miles wide at its narrowest; Wood Mackenzie says the closure removed more than 80 million tonnes a year of LNG, roughly 20% of world supply.

Insurers want evidence the agreement is holding before pricing normalises: 'It's not something that happens overnight.' Later reporting (June 28) says a ceasefire was undermined by renewed hostilities on June 27.
why_it_matters: Ships need war-risk cover to move. If the price stays high after a deal, shipping costs, energy prices and delivery times may stay elevated even when a strait is formally open.

title: Sixfold Launches AI Underwriter for P&C Insurers, Offering Optional Straight-Through Quote and Bind With Human Oversight
summary: Insurtech Sixfold launched its AI Underwriter on June 15, 2026; vendor-reported results include 50% to 97% faster processing, with each carrier deciding how much the agent handles autonomously.
description:
An AI system that reads insurance submissions, judges them against an insurer's appetite and, if the insurer allows, prepares them for quoting and binding is now available commercially. Sixfold, an insurtech company, launched its AI Underwriter on June 15, 2026, for property and casualty insurers, according to an announcement covered by Insurance Edge and The Insurer. This article summarises that coverage. Nearly all the figures about performance come from Sixfold itself and from customer testimonials in its announcement, and have not been independently verified, which is why this article labels them as the vendor's claims. An earlier version of this article described the agent as autonomous. The announcement stresses that underwriters keep direction, judgment and accountability, and that each carrier decides how much the agent does on its own, so that wording has been corrected.

What does it do? According to the announcement, the AI Underwriter extracts and cleans data from a submission, flags missing information, assesses appetite and portfolio fit, and considers what it has learned about the broker and risk class. It then gives a recommendation with its rationale and suggests a next step. When configured for straight-through processing, it produces quote- and bind-ready materials for a broker or customer to accept. A submission is the package of information a broker sends an insurer when seeking cover for a client, often a mix of forms, emails and attachments that must be reviewed before a quote. Reducing that manual work is the main aim.

How is it trained? Sixfold describes a shared foundation called the Underwriting Brain, trained on professional credential standards, underwriter reasoning patterns and a curated library of ground-truth examples. On top of that, each carrier's instance learns from its own underwriters' decisions. Sixfold says one carrier's data never trains another's. That claim is important to insurers worried about confidentiality and competitive information, but it is a statement by the vendor, and we have not seen an independent audit.

What results does Sixfold report? Since launching in 2023, it says it has processed more than 1.5 million submissions across more than 50 lines of business in North America, South America, the UK, Europe and Australia. Its customers include Skyward Specialty, Zurich, Generali GC&C, Guardian, AXIS and New York Life, which together represent $270 billion in gross written premium. Reported results, described as historical and vendor-stated, include 50% to 97% faster processing, hit ratios up 15% or more, and up to 30% higher gross written premium per underwriter. Sixfold also says loss and expense ratios improve over time. At Skyward Specialty, early results reportedly showed the tool performed most of the underwriting analysis, and Sixfold says customers see 90% or higher underwriting adoption, meaning actual users compared with expected users. The range of 50% to 97% is very wide, and the announcement does not explain what drives the difference, so readers should not expect any single insurer to see a particular figure.

Who is in charge? The announcement says underwriters provide direction and judgment, guide exceptions and remain accountable for governance of the tool. Each carrier decides how much work the agent handles autonomously. Sixfold cites a responsible AI programme with governance controls and regulatory relationships to support deployment across regions. Its chief operating officer, Jane Tran, is quoted as saying, "The AI Underwriter works every case as a colleague." That framing presents the product as support for underwriters, not as a replacement for them.

What questions does this raise? First, accuracy and bias: an AI that recommends declining a risk must be explainable and tested. The announcement says the agent gives a rationale, which helps, but it does not describe testing or audit methods. Second, regulation: insurance regulators in many jurisdictions are developing rules on the use of AI and data in underwriting, and carriers remain responsible for decisions. Third, accountability when things go wrong. Fourth, whether faster quoting leads to better outcomes or simply more volume.

What does it mean for brokers and customers? Faster responses on submissions could shorten the time to get a quote, especially for smaller commercial risks that insurers sometimes find uneconomic to underwrite manually. Brokers may find that clearer appetite signals reduce wasted submissions. On the other hand, customers whose risks do not fit an insurer's pattern may be declined faster. These effects are possibilities and have not been measured in the sources reviewed.

How does this compare with other uses of AI in insurance? Many insurers already use automation for personal lines such as car and home insurance, where data is standardised. Commercial and specialty submissions are less uniform, which is why a product aimed at reading messy documents and applying an insurer's own appetite is notable. Other vendors offer similar tools, and Marsh's report on AI exclusions, covered elsewhere on this site, shows that insurers are also working out how to cover the risks that AI itself creates.

This is an announcement of a new product, and its real impact will become clear as insurers publish their own results. This article is not an endorsement of any vendor or investment advice.
source_name: Sixfold launch announcement (via Insurance Edge) and The Insurer
image_alt: Artificial intelligence transforming insurance underwriting workflows (illustrative)
key_points: Sixfold launched its AI Underwriter on June 15, 2026 for property and casualty insurers; it raised a $30 million Series B in January to build it.

The agent extracts and cleans submission data, flags missing information, assesses appetite and portfolio fit, and recommends a next step with its rationale; when configured, it can produce quote- and bind-ready materials.
Underwriters provide direction and judgment and remain accountable, and each carrier decides how much work the agent handles autonomously.

Sixfold says it has processed more than 1.5 million submissions across 50+ lines since 2023; customers include Zurich, Generali GC&C, Guardian, AXIS, Skyward Specialty and New York Life, together representing $270 billion in GWP.
Performance claims (50% to 97% faster processing, hit ratios up 15% or more, up to 30% higher GWP per underwriter) come from Sixfold and have not been independently verified.
why_it_matters: Underwriting is the core decision insurers make. If AI agents can handle submissions faster and consistently, they could change how commercial insurance is bought and sold, but they also raise questions about accountability, accuracy and fairness.

title: IRDAI Ties Insurer Executives' Variable Pay to Claims, Grievances and Dark-Pattern Removal in New Governance Circular
summary: IRDAI's May 25, 2026 circular amending its 2024 master circular on corporate governance makes six customer- and soundness-related parameters worth 50% of the assessment for variable pay of key management personnel, effective from FY 2026-27.
description:
India's insurance regulator wants insurers' bosses to be paid, in part, for how well they treat customers. A circular issued by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) on May 25, 2026, amends its master circular on corporate governance for insurers, first issued in 2024, to tie the variable pay and incentives of key management personnel and senior management to customer-centric and soundness measures. According to Outlook Money and the Mondaq legal commentary, the amendment takes effect from the 2026-27 financial year. This article summarises those reports. An earlier version said the circular took effect immediately and described it as amending the 2024 Regulations themselves. The reports we reviewed describe an amendment to the 2024 master circular, with application from FY 2026-27, so the article has been corrected.

What are the new parameters? Six core parameters together carry a 50% weightage in determining variable pay. They are overall financial soundness, product performance, claims responsiveness, grievance redressal, implementation of Indian Accounting Standards, and the removal of dark patterns in insurer and distributor customer interactions. Outlook Money reports that implementation of Indian Accounting Standards and removal of dark patterns each carry 10%, while it does not give individual weights for the other four. The remaining 50% of the assessment is left to insurers, who base it on their own business priorities and the individual executive's role. The reports do not state what proportion of total pay is variable, and they do not describe deferral or clawback rules, so readers should not assume the circular includes them.

What are dark patterns? The term refers to website and app designs that steer users into choices they might not otherwise make, for example by hiding opt-outs, making cancellation difficult or pre-ticking extra products. Including them in executive pay metrics means that leaders would be assessed on the removal of such practices from insurer and distributor channels.

What extra measures apply by type of insurer? According to Outlook Money, life insurers will be assessed on indicators such as renewal premium ratios, persistency, expense management and assets under management. General insurers and standalone health insurers will be assessed on incurred loss ratios, renewal business ratios and expense management indicators. These line-specific measures sit alongside the six core parameters.

What must insurers disclose? The disclosure rules are detailed. On claims, insurers must report the share of claims settled within 15, 30, 60 and more than 60 days, and the numbers of claims fully paid, partially paid, rejected, repudiated or pending, with monthly updates. On grievances, they must report complaints resolved within the specified timelines and those still unresolved, also monthly. A service request unresolved for more than seven days may be treated as a grievance. Financial soundness disclosures are updated quarterly. Insurers must post executive-pay performance information on their websites in a simple, accessible format, and must not ask users for personal details simply to view the disclosures. Mondaq adds that insurers must disclose the parameters behind pay for key management personnel and directors, report performance against those parameters and make prior-year information available.

What is the role of boards? Nomination and remuneration committees must coordinate with risk management committees when designing senior management pay policies. Mondaq says boards and remuneration committees will be expected to demonstrate that executive incentives reflect policyholder interests, conduct risk and long-term governance objectives. In practice, that means that a bonus structure that rewards premium growth alone will be harder to defend.

How have insurers reacted? Business Standard's headline describes insurers as wary, and the circular is characterised as a tightening of an already demanding framework. We have not seen published statements from named insurers in the sources reviewed, so this article does not attribute any particular view to a specific company.

What does it mean for policyholders? If the measures work as intended, claims handling and complaint resolution become part of how insurers' leaders are judged financially. Public monthly data would let customers and journalists compare insurers on settlement speed and complaint resolution. The effect will depend on how consistently insurers report and how closely IRDAI checks the data. A weighting of 50% sounds large, but the way each parameter is scored is left to the insurer's remuneration framework, and the reports do not describe a standard scoring method.

For insurers, the practical work is in building the data systems to track claims timing and complaints accurately, because the same figures will now be published and used to decide pay. Smaller insurers may find the reporting burden heavier than larger ones, a point the reports do not address directly.

More broadly, linking pay to conduct is a trend in financial regulation globally. The Indian approach is notable because it names specific consumer outcomes, such as claim timelines. Whether it improves experience for policyholders will become clearer after the first full year of disclosures in 2026-27. This article reports published summaries of the circular and is not legal advice; insurers and advisers should read the circular itself.
source_name: IRDAI circular (via Mondaq, Outlook Money and Business Standard reporting)
image_alt: India insurance regulation linking executive pay to claims and customer outcomes (illustrative)
key_points: IRDAI issued the circular on May 25, 2026, amending its 2024 master circular on corporate governance for insurers; it takes effect from FY 2026-27.

Six parameters together carry 50% weightage in deciding variable pay: financial soundness, product performance, claims responsiveness, grievance redressal, Indian Accounting Standards implementation (10%) and removal of dark patterns (10%).
Insurers decide the remaining 50% based on business priorities and each executive's role; life insurers and general and health insurers have additional line-specific indicators.
Insurers must publish claims settlement timing (within 15, 30, 60 and more days) and grievance data monthly, and financial soundness data quarterly, without asking users for personal details.
Nomination and remuneration committees must coordinate with risk management committees when designing senior management pay.
why_it_matters: Executive pay shapes behaviour. By linking bonuses to claim payment and complaint handling, India's regulator is trying to make policyholder outcomes, not only growth, a financial priority for insurer leaders.

title: SoftBank's PayPay to Buy 70.2% of T&D Financial Life for About ¥134.3 Billion, With Closing Planned for October 2027
summary: PayPay agreed on June 4, 2026 to buy 70.2% of T&D Financial Life Insurance from T&D Holdings for about ¥134.3 billion ($840 million), with the share transfer planned for October 1, 2027 and subject to conditions.
description:
One of Japan's most-used payment apps is buying a life insurer. On June 4, 2026, PayPay, the SoftBank-backed company, agreed to acquire a 70.2% stake in T&D Financial Life Insurance from T&D Holdings for about ¥134.3 billion, or roughly $840 million, according to reporting by The Next Web and the Japan Times. This article summarises that reporting. An earlier version of this article said the deal was funded partly by proceeds from PayPay's US listing. The report we reviewed says PayPay will fund the 70.2% stake from its own cash. PayPay did list American depositary shares on Nasdaq in March 2026, raising about $880 million, and that context is described below.

What are the deal terms? The board resolution and contract were signed on June 4, and the share transfer is planned for October 1, 2027. That is a long gap, and the closing depends on conditions: T&D Financial Life must complete a move to International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) accounting, and regulatory approvals are required. Either could change the timetable. The ownership structure after the deal is also set out. OneIM Indigo Holdings, an affiliate of One Investment Management, is expected to take 14.9%, and T&D Holdings will keep the remaining 14.9%. PayPay and OneIM have said they are independent stakeholders with no joint voting or coordinated share-transfer agreement. PayPay holds a call option over T&D's 14.9% after the transfer, while T&D holds a put option that it can exercise three years after signing.

What is being acquired? T&D Financial Life is a life insurer owned by T&D Holdings. The report says it reported net income of ¥8.2 billion in its latest fiscal year, up from ¥5.6 billion, and had total assets of about ¥1.96 trillion as of March 31, 2026. For comparison, a price of ¥134.3 billion for 70.2% implies a value of around ¥191 billion for the whole company, a figure we have calculated from the stated price and stake and which the companies have not stated themselves.

Why is PayPay doing it? PayPay already offers payments, credit, banking and securities, and it reported more than 74 million registered users as of May 2026. It sees life insurance as a way to extend its app across customers' life stages. The broader alliance with SoftBank includes selling partner products, such as those of Taiyo Life, through the app, deploying SoftBank's AI in call centres, and developing health and senior-care initiatives. The Next Web frames the deal as a shift from moving money to holding it, meaning that PayPay would hold long-term policyholder funds and not only pass payments through.

What does the listing have to do with it? PayPay listed on Nasdaq in March 2026 at $16 per share, raising about $880 million, and SoftBank remains its consolidated parent. The listing gives PayPay a public currency and more visibility, but the report says the purchase itself will be funded from its own cash, so readers should not assume the listing money was used.

What are the risks and questions? First, timing. A closing more than 16 months after signing leaves room for changes in markets, regulation or strategy. Second, integration. Selling life insurance is different from selling a payment or a loan: products are more complex, mis-selling rules are strict, and customers expect advice. Third, regulation. Japan's Financial Services Agency will review the deal, and the IFRS transition is itself a condition. The reports do not describe the regulator's likely view, and we have not seen any statement from it. Fourth, the economics: life insurers earn money over decades, while app businesses are used to quicker cycles.

Why might it matter for competitors? Japan's life insurers have relied heavily on sales agents, bank branches and corporate channels. A platform with tens of millions of users and data on spending could offer a different route to customers, especially younger ones. Whether customers will buy life cover through a payment app is not yet clear, and the evidence from other markets is mixed.

What should customers of T&D Financial Life expect? Nothing changes immediately. Policies already issued remain contracts with the insurer, and the deal is a change in ownership, not a transfer of policies. Japanese regulators generally focus on policyholder protection when ownership of an insurer changes, and any approval process would look at the buyer's financial strength and governance. Customers would normally be told about changes to their policy servicing through the insurer itself. Because the closing is planned for late 2027, any changes to products or distribution are likely to come after that date.

What should observers watch? Three things stand out: whether the IFRS transition and approvals proceed on schedule, how PayPay describes its insurance strategy in its regular reporting as a listed company, and whether competing platforms in Japan and elsewhere announce similar moves. Each would help show whether this is a one-off transaction or the start of a wider trend of fintech apps owning insurers.

For now, this is an agreed deal, not a completed one. Readers should treat the plans for AI and cross-selling as intentions described by the companies. This article reports published information and is not investment advice.
source_name: SoftBank / The Next Web and Japan Times reporting
image_alt: Japanese payments super-app expanding into life insurance (illustrative)
key_points: PayPay agreed to buy a 70.2% stake in T&D Financial Life Insurance from T&D Holdings for about ¥134.3 billion (roughly $840 million); the contract was signed June 4, 2026.
The share transfer is planned for October 1, 2027, and depends on T&D Financial Life moving to IFRS accounting and on regulatory approvals.
OneIM Indigo Holdings, an affiliate of One Investment Management, is expected to take 14.9%, and T&D Holdings keeps 14.9%; PayPay has a call option and T&D a put option on that stake.
T&D Financial Life reported net income of ¥8.2 billion in its latest fiscal year (¥5.6 billion before) and total assets of about ¥1.96 trillion at March 31, 2026.
PayPay had over 74 million registered users in May 2026 and plans to sell partner products, including Taiyo Life's, and deploy SoftBank AI in call centres.
why_it_matters: A payments app with tens of millions of users is moving into life insurance. If it works, it could change how Japanese consumers buy protection and how traditional life insurers distribute products, though the deal is more than a year from closing.

title: Australia's Home Insurance Squeeze: Premiums Up 51% in Five Years and a Line That Still Struggles to Make an Underwriting Profit
summary: APRA data to March 2026 show householders insurance earning about $4.25 billion of quarterly premium yet slipping into underwriting losses in four of ten quarters, while average premiums rose 51% between 2020 and late 2025.
description:
Australian home insurance is caught between two pressures: premiums that households find increasingly hard to afford, and results that remain volatile for insurers even after years of increases. The picture comes from the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority's quarterly general insurance statistics, released on May 29, 2026 for the period to March 2026, as analysed by Insurance Business Australia, together with data from the consultancy Finity, the comparison site Canstar and the Insurance Council of Australia. This article summarises that analysis. An earlier version cited a survey and a report that do not appear in the source and have been removed.

Start with the insurers' side. Householders insurance, which covers the building and sometimes contents of owner-occupied homes, collected gross written premium of $3.82 billion in the December 2023 quarter and $4.49 billion in the December 2025 quarter, an increase of 17.4%, according to the APRA data in the article. Despite that growth, the line often loses money on underwriting. The householders insurance service result, which is the profit or loss from insurance activities, was negative in four of the ten quarters examined. The worst was the December 2025 quarter, with a loss of $1.08 billion, when net claims used up nearly 80% of premiums. The March 2026 quarter was close to break-even, with a negative $10 million on $4.25 billion of quarterly premium. The swings are linked to the timing of catastrophes: the June 2025 quarter showed a profit of $711 million, while the December 2025 quarter was the large loss.

Now the customers' side. Finity data cited in the article show that the average home premium rose 51% from 2020 to October 2025, from $1,940 to $2,938. Canstar figures show a further rise of 14% in 2025. These increases have far outpaced the growth of most household incomes. The Australia Institute estimated that about 1.4 million homes were uninsured or underinsured in 2025. APRA's climate vulnerability assessment found premiums rose an average of 7.2% a year from 2010 to 2025, against wage growth of 3.1%, and that about one in seven houses is uninsured today, which could rise to about one in four by 2050. These figures come from a separate Insurance Business report.

What explains the cost? The Insurance Council of Australia, the industry's trade body, points to several factors. Extreme weather is one: it says extreme weather events in 2025 cost $4.8 billion in insured losses from 294,000 claims. Another is development in high-risk areas, where more homes are built in places exposed to floods and fires. A third is the cost of rebuilding: it cites a 40% rise in building material costs since 2022, and asset values that have grown. The fourth is tax. The Council says that in New South Wales, up to 37% of a premium is tax once GST, stamp duty and the Emergency Services Levy are included. The article makes a practical point for brokers and homeowners: a building insured for $800,000 in 2021 might cost $1.1 million to rebuild now, so sums insured should be reviewed to avoid underinsurance.

Equity is a central concern. The Insurance Council says high flood risk is correlated with lower socioeconomic status, and reports that around 70% of households with the highest flood exposure live in areas where median income is below the national median. If those households face the steepest premiums and the greatest risk, they are also the ones least able to absorb a disaster. This is the group for which premium rises can lead to dropping cover, and the consequences fall on the household and any lender.

The policy responses discussed are about reducing the underlying risk and cost. Resilience and mitigation, for example flood levees, fire breaks and stormwater infrastructure, can reduce expected losses and therefore premiums over time, as can planning rules that steer development away from high-risk locations. Reducing taxes and levies on insurance is another option the industry raises, although governments rely on those revenues. The article argues that pricing pressure is likely to intensify.

What can homeowners do now? Check that the sum insured reflects the current cost of rebuilding, including higher building costs, since being underinsured can leave a gap after a total loss. Compare quotes, as prices vary significantly between insurers. Ask about discounts for mitigation measures such as upgrading roofs or installing flood barriers. Understand the excess and any exclusions, particularly for flood, which is defined differently by different insurers. If you are struggling to pay, speak to your insurer before cover lapses, because a gap in cover can be costly.

For lenders, regulators and governments, the data point to a sustained problem and not a one-off. The insurance line is growing in premium but not reliably earning an underwriting profit, which limits how much insurers can absorb before prices rise again. At the same time, household affordability is under strain from interest rates. The next APRA statistics, covering the June 2026 quarter, will show whether the March result of close to break-even was the start of a recovery or a lull between catastrophes.
source_name: Insurance Business Australia (citing APRA, Finity, Canstar and the Insurance Council of Australia)
image_alt: Australian home insurance affordability and climate risk pressures (illustrative)
key_points: APRA's statistics to March 2026, released on May 29, show householders gross written premium rising from $3.82 billion in December 2023 to $4.49 billion in December 2025, up 17.4%.

The householders insurance service result was negative in four of the ten quarters reviewed, with a $1.08 billion loss in December 2025 and a loss of about $10 million on $4.25 billion of premium in March 2026.
Finity data cited by Insurance Business show the average home premium rose 51% from 2020 to October 2025, from $1,940 to $2,938, and Canstar figures show a further 14% rise in 2025.

The Insurance Council attributes pressure to extreme weather (A$4.8 billion of insured losses from 294,000 claims in 2025), a 40% rise in building costs since 2022, and taxes that in New South Wales can be up to 37% of a premium.

The Australia Institute estimates about 1.4 million homes were uninsured or underinsured in 2025, and APRA's climate assessment says about one in seven houses is uninsured, rising to about one in four by 2050.
why_it_matters: Home insurance is a condition of most mortgages, so a market where cover is increasingly unaffordable is a risk for households, lenders and governments. The data show that rising premiums have not yet made the line reliably profitable, which suggests prices and affordability pressures will continue.

title: UK Motor Insurers Head Back Toward Losses: Oxbow Forecasts Profit to Fall From About £2 Billion to £1.3 Billion in 2026 as Repair Costs Bite
summary: Insurance Business (June 9, 2026) reports Oxbow Partners forecasting UK motor profit falling to £1.3 billion in 2026 and a combined ratio of 95%, while EY projects 111%, as premiums fell in 2025 and repair costs rise.
description:
UK motor insurance has gone from record profits to forecasts of falling margins within a year. Insurance Business reported on June 9, 2026, on the findings of consultancy Oxbow Partners and others: the sector made a record operating profit of about £2 billion in 2025, helped by price increases in 2023 and 2024, and is expected to see profits fall in 2026. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article said that average quoted premiums rose 4.5% in the first quarter, citing Consumer Intelligence, and called the rise the first quarterly increase since early 2024. We could not confirm the Consumer Intelligence figure in the sources reviewed, so it has been replaced with the Pearson Ham figure, which shows a 1% rate increase across the first quarter of 2026. Readers should treat the direction of prices as a matter on which sources differ.

What does Oxbow forecast? In its UK Motor Market Report 2026, which covers 19 of the largest insurers, roughly 90% of the market, Oxbow forecasts that profit will fall to £1.3 billion in 2026 and decline further in 2027. It expects the combined ratio to rise from 89% in 2025 to 95% in 2026 and 96% in 2027. The loss ratio, the share of premiums paid out in claims, is forecast to rise from 66% to 71%. Gross earned premium is expected to fall 2% in 2026, while claims costs rise 5%. The expense ratio is forecast to rise slightly to 24% in 2026. A combined ratio below 100% means the insurer makes an underwriting profit, so Oxbow's forecast is for a narrowing of profit and not a loss.

What happened in 2025? Average premiums fell 9% in 2025, much more than Oxbow's estimate of 3%. Claims inflation eased to 3% from 10% in 2024. The sector's record profit came from the earlier price increases flowing through into earned premiums while claims inflation cooled. That combination cannot last: when prices fall faster than claims costs, margins narrow.

How does EY see it? EY is more pessimistic. It projects net combined ratios of 101% for 2025 and 111% for 2026. EY's Dan Beard said the outlook had deteriorated further than expected. The difference between Oxbow's 95% and EY's 111% is large and probably reflects different definitions and methods: EY's figure is a net combined ratio, and the two firms may use different samples and assumptions. The article does not explain the gap, so we do not try to reconcile the two. A reader should treat them as a range of views, from a modest decline in profit to a return to underwriting losses.

What are the signals on rates and claims? Pearson Ham data shows a 1% rate increase across the first quarter of 2026, a sign that prices may be turning. The Association of British Insurers (ABI) reports that the average accidental damage claim rose 8% to £3,699 in the first quarter of 2026. Repair costs accounted for 64% of motor claims in the third quarter of 2025, totalling £1.9 billion. The article also notes that the Iran conflict could add energy-driven inflation to repair and parts costs, though it does not quantify the effect.

Why might cycles be shorter? Oxbow points to structural changes. The General Insurance Pricing Practices rules, which ban pricing practices that penalise loyal customers, speed up rate corrections because insurers cannot rely on long-standing customers to carry price increases. Consolidation, including Aviva and Direct Line, Ageas and esure, and Saga's insurance operations, is also expected to affect competition. Together, Oxbow expects these to produce shorter, less volatile pricing cycles, with the combined ratio hovering in the mid-90s. That is a forecast and not an established fact.

What does it mean for drivers? If margins narrow as forecast, insurers will probably stop cutting prices and may raise them. Drivers who have enjoyed lower renewal quotes could see that change, so shopping around before renewal remains sensible. Specific premiums depend on the driver, car and area, and none of the figures in the report applies to an individual. The report does not forecast the size of increases, and we do not offer one.

What does it mean for insurers? A profit of £1.3 billion is still substantial, but the direction is downward, and the insurers that control repair costs, manage claims well and price accurately should fare better. Costs include parts and labour for modern vehicles that are expensive to repair, which is a long-term pressure on the sector.

One caution on the numbers: the report mixes forecasts from different organisations, actual data from the ABI and a pricing tracker, and a headline about a £700 million fall in profit that is simply the gap between about £2 billion and £1.3 billion. Because forecasts depend on assumptions about claims inflation, competition and the economy, they may be revised, particularly if the Middle East conflict affects parts and energy costs.

This article reports published forecasts and survey data and is not financial advice.
source_name: Insurance Business UK (Oxbow Partners UK Motor Market Report 2026; EY; ABI; Pearson Ham)
image_alt: UK car insurance premiums rising on repair-cost inflation (illustrative)
key_points: The UK motor sector posted a record operating profit of about £2 billion in 2025, helped by price increases in 2023 and 2024; Oxbow forecasts £1.3 billion in 2026 and a further decline in 2027.
Oxbow expects the combined ratio to rise from 89% in 2025 to 95% in 2026 and 96% in 2027, and the loss ratio from 66% to 71%.
Average premiums fell 9% in 2025 (Oxbow had estimated 3%); claims inflation eased to 3% from 10% in 2024.
EY is more pessimistic, projecting net combined ratios of 101% for 2025 and 111% for 2026; Pearson Ham data shows a 1% rate rise across Q1 2026.
The ABI says the average accidental damage claim rose 8% to £3,699 in Q1 2026, and repair costs made up 64% of motor claims (£1.9 billion) in Q3 2025.
why_it_matters: After years of high premiums, UK drivers may see prices rise again if insurers' margins narrow as forecast. The reasons, rising repair costs and falling prices in 2025, show how quickly motor insurance cycles can turn.

title: Fairview and UnitedHealthcare: How a Medicare Advantage Contract Dispute Reached Court Ahead of 2027 Open Enrollment
summary: Fairview Health Services did not renew its UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage contract in June 2026 and sued on October 7 over 2027 plan listings; about 33,000 Fairview patients are enrolled in UnitedHealthcare MA plans each year.
description:
A contract dispute between a Minnesota health system and the largest Medicare Advantage insurer in the United States has moved from negotiating rooms to a federal courtroom. Fairview Health Services, based in Minneapolis, and UnitedHealthcare have been at odds for more than a year over Medicare Advantage contracts, and on October 7, 2026, Fairview sued, according to MPR News. This article was first written in June 2026, when the dispute was a contract impasse. It has been updated with later reporting and keeps the original publication date because it is an upgrade of that article. The situation is changing, and readers should check for current news before making decisions about coverage. An earlier version of this article said that Medicare Advantage covers slightly more than half of US seniors and described UnitedHealthcare's calling the early notice a scare tactic. We could not verify those two points in the sources reviewed, so they have been removed.

What happened first? InsuranceNewsNet reported in November 2025 that Fairview and UnitedHealthcare had reached a one-year contract that kept Medicare Advantage patients, including seniors with employer retiree coverage, in network. Fairview said it chose the deal in the interest of stability for Minnesota seniors, but still had concerns about UnitedHealthcare's approach, and that the deal was not the same proposal UnitedHealthcare had offered before. At the time, Fairview said claims denials and prior authorisation requirements imposed significant costs on the health system. UnitedHealthcare denied that its denial rates were high, defended its practices, and accused Fairview of making false claims and using patients as a bargaining chip. About 33,000 Medicare Advantage beneficiaries could have lost access to the system in 2026. For context, about 653,000 Minnesotans use Medicare Advantage plans from several insurers, and UCare left the state's Medicare Advantage market on January 1, 2026, forcing at least 158,000 Minnesotans to find new coverage.

What happened in 2026? According to MPR News, Fairview did not renew its contract with UnitedHealthcare in June. Fairview says it has had problems with UnitedHealthcare's Medicare Advantage plans for years, including payment delays, low reimbursement rates, prior authorisation difficulties and claim denials. In September, Fairview asked UnitedHealthcare to confirm that Fairview would not appear in 2027 provider directories. According to Fairview, UnitedHealthcare seemed surprised and could not answer. Fairview then requested written confirmation and sent a notice that it would not participate in UnitedHealthcare's Medicare Advantage plans in 2027.

What is the lawsuit about? Fairview filed suit in federal court in Minnesota, alleging false advertising of UnitedHealthcare's 2027 Medicare Advantage plans. Fairview says UnitedHealthcare's annual notice directs enrollees to an online directory that still lists Fairview as in-network. The notice also says enrollment continues automatically if members do not select another plan. Fairview argues that this could lead patients to renew believing they keep Fairview access. The filing says Fairview is not currently negotiating with UnitedHealthcare and does not expect to reopen talks. These are allegations in a lawsuit, and the court has not decided them.

What does Fairview want? It seeks a temporary restraining order before Medicare's annual enrollment period begins on October 15, an order requiring UnitedHealthcare to correct its network information, the turnover of profits UnitedHealthcare earns from Fairview patients who enroll in its 2027 plans, and compensatory damages for the cost of outreach to Medicare patients. Fairview's chief medical officer, Dr Jaya Kumar, said: "We are asking the court to require accurate information before enrollment begins."

What does UnitedHealthcare say? According to the report, UnitedHealthcare says it is working with Fairview in good faith toward an affordable agreement that preserves long-term member access. If no deal is reached, it says members will be notified about possible out-of-network status, following guidelines from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

Who is affected? Fairview estimates that about 33,000 of its current patients are enrolled in UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage plans each year. Open enrollment runs from October 15 to December 7. The lawsuit does not affect Fairview's separate commercial agreement with UnitedHealthcare, so members with employer-sponsored UnitedHealthcare coverage keep in-network access to Fairview in 2027. UnitedHealthcare is the largest Medicare Advantage insurer nationally and, according to the November 2025 report, projected its business would shrink by one million people in 2026.

Why do these disputes happen? Hospitals and insurers negotiate payment rates and rules for approvals. Health systems often argue that prior authorisation and denials add administrative cost and delay care, while insurers argue that such controls limit unnecessary spending. Medicare Advantage plans are paid by the federal government, and each year plans and providers decide whether to stay in network. When talks fail near open enrollment, patients are caught between the two sides.

What should seniors do? Anyone in a UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage plan who uses Fairview should confirm network status directly with both the plan and the provider, in writing if possible, before the December 7 deadline. Medicare's own plan finder and the State Health Insurance Assistance Program can help people compare alternatives. This is general information about a developing dispute and not individual advice. The facts above are drawn from published reports and court filings described by the news media.
image_alt: US Medicare Advantage insurer and hospital contract dispute (illustrative)
key_points: In November 2025, Fairview and UnitedHealthcare agreed a one-year contract that kept Medicare Advantage patients in network; about 33,000 Fairview-related MA beneficiaries had been at risk of losing access.
Fairview did not renew the contract in June 2026, citing payment delays, low reimbursement, prior authorisation difficulties and claim denials, which UnitedHealthcare disputes.

On October 7, 2026, Fairview sued in federal court in Minnesota, alleging false advertising because UnitedHealthcare's 2027 materials direct members to a directory that still lists Fairview as in-network.

Fairview seeks a restraining order before Medicare open enrollment starts October 15, a correction of network information and damages; UnitedHealthcare says it is working in good faith toward an agreement.
The dispute does not affect Fairview's separate commercial agreement with UnitedHealthcare, so employer-sponsored members keep in-network access in 2027.
why_it_matters: Medicare Advantage members choose plans partly on which doctors and hospitals are in network. A contract dispute close to open enrollment can leave seniors unsure whether they will keep access to their usual care.

title: LIMRA: US Annuity Sales Hold at $104.6 Billion, a 10th Straight $100 Billion Quarter, as New Life Premium Rises 10% in Q1 2026
summary: LIMRA's preliminary Q1 2026 data show annuity sales of $104.6 billion (down 2%), RILA sales up 21% to $21.2 billion, and new annualised life premium up 10% to $4.5 billion.
description:
Americans bought more than $100 billion of annuities for the tenth quarter in a row, according to preliminary data from LIMRA, the life insurance and retirement industry research group. Total US annuity sales were $104.6 billion in the first quarter of 2026, down 2% from a year earlier, with the data covering 87% of the market. LIMRA's Bryan Hodgens said the threshold for annuity sales appears to have stabilised above $100 billion. A separate LIMRA report, covered by Insurance Business, shows that new life insurance premium also rose strongly. This article summarises both. An earlier version of this article did not make clear that the annuity total was slightly lower than a year earlier; it fell 2%, and the article now says so. The data are preliminary and may be revised. The earlier version also attributed annuity and RILA figures to the Insurance Business life report, which does not contain them; they come from LIMRA's own annuity release.

Which annuities are selling? Registered index-linked annuities, known as RILAs, were the standout. Sales rose 21% to $21.2 billion, the second-highest quarter on record and the 30th straight quarter of year-over-year growth. LIMRA forecasts that 2026 RILA sales will exceed the record set in 2025. A RILA gives buyers a return linked to a market index with a degree of downside protection, but, unlike a fixed annuity, it can lose value in a falling market within set limits. Traditional variable annuities rose 9% to $16.1 billion, their third consecutive quarter of year-over-year growth.

Other categories fell. Fixed-rate deferred annuities, which pay a set interest rate, were down 16% to $34 billion, though still about a third of the total market. Fixed indexed annuities (FIAs) were $26.6 billion, down 4%. Single premium immediate annuities (SPIAs), which turn a lump sum into immediate income, rose 22% to $3.7 billion, and deferred income annuities rose 6% to $1 billion. Together these figures suggest buyers are moving some money from fixed products to those linked to markets or to income, though LIMRA's release does not explain the reasons, and we do not offer one.

How is life insurance doing? According to LIMRA's preliminary data reported by Insurance Business, total new annualised premium plus excess was $4.5 billion in the first quarter, up 10% year over year, with the policy count up 9%. A year earlier the figure was $3.9 billion. LIMRA forecasts growth of 2% to 6% in 2026, compared with a long-run average of 3.1%, so the first quarter is well ahead of that range. Full-year 2025 new annualised premium exceeded $17.5 billion, up 10%, a record.

By product, whole life made up 36% of the market, with new premium up 9% to $1.6 billion and policy count up 13%. Indexed universal life (IUL) premium rose 14% to $1.1 billion, or 25% of the total, and six of the top ten IUL carriers posted double-digit policy growth. Variable universal life premium rose 12% to $729 million. Term life premium rose 9% to $788 million. Fixed universal life fell 6% to $221 million, its sixth straight quarterly decline. IUL is a life insurance product, not an annuity, and these figures should not be combined with the annuity data.

What do LIMRA's analysts say? Sean Grindall of LIMRA said demand for life insurance has not waned despite consumer financial worries. Karen Terry of LIMRA noted that many traditional whole life carriers are seeing flat to negative growth, and credited whole life's strength largely to final expense products, which are smaller policies designed to pay funeral and end-of-life costs. That comment is a useful caution: growth at the market level does not mean that every insurer is doing well.

Why do these numbers matter? Annuities are a major route by which insurers collect long-term funds that they invest in bonds and other assets. High sales help explain why insurers have expanded into private credit and other assets, a trend covered elsewhere on this site by Moody's report. Consumers who buy an annuity are relying on the insurer's financial strength for decades, so the stability of the insurer matters as much as the product features.

What should buyers consider? Annuities differ greatly. Fixed annuities offer a stated rate, but the rate may not keep pace with inflation. RILAs and variable annuities carry market risk, fees and surrender charges. Immediate annuities pay income but are usually irreversible. Buyers should compare the insurer's financial strength rating, the fees, the surrender period and the guarantees, and consider whether the product suits their goals. An independent adviser who is paid by fee and not by commission can help, though the quality of advice varies.

It is worth remembering that sales are not the same as assets or profits. A record quarter of RILA sales means insurers are taking in new money on those products, but the performance of each product depends on markets and on how well the insurer hedges its promises. LIMRA's figures describe the flow of new business, and say nothing about customer satisfaction or the value the products deliver.

This article summarises industry sales data and is general information. It is not financial or investment advice, and past sales do not predict future trends.
source_name: LIMRA (annuity and life insurance sales, Q1 2026) via Insurance Business
image_alt: US life insurance and annuity sales momentum in 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: US annuity sales were $104.6 billion in Q1 2026, down 2% year over year, the tenth consecutive quarter above $100 billion; LIMRA says the threshold 'appears to be stabilized above $100 billion'.
Registered index-linked annuity (RILA) sales rose 21% to $21.2 billion, the second-highest quarter on record and the 30th straight quarter of year-over-year growth.
Fixed-rate deferred annuities fell 16% to $34 billion and fixed indexed annuities fell 4% to $26.6 billion; traditional variable annuities rose 9% to $16.1 billion.
New annualised life insurance premium rose 10% to $4.5 billion, with policy count up 9%; LIMRA forecasts 2026 growth of 2% to 6%.
Whole life made up 36% of the market, indexed universal life 25% (up 14% to $1.1 billion); fixed universal life fell 6% for a sixth straight decline.
why_it_matters: Annuities and life insurance are how many Americans secure retirement income and protect their families. Shifts between product types show how consumers respond to interest rates, market risk and the need for guaranteed income.

title: Great Eastern Named Singapore's Only Brand in Brand Finance's Insurance 100 2026, With US$4.9 Billion Brand Value and an AAA Strength Rating
summary: Brand Finance's Insurance 100 2026, published June 9, ranks Great Eastern 33rd by brand value (US$4.9 billion, up 2%) and 11th for brand strength (81.4/100, AAA); the top 100 insurance brands grew 14% to US$606.7 billion.
description:
Singapore's Great Eastern has been recognised as one of the strongest insurance brands in the world by a brand valuation consultancy. In its Insurance 100 2026 report, published on June 9, 2026, Brand Finance valued Great Eastern's brand at US$4.9 billion, up 2% from the previous year. That placed it 33rd among the sector's top 100 brands by value. On brand strength, a score that measures how well a brand performs on factors such as familiarity, loyalty and perceived quality, Great Eastern scored 81.4 out of 100, which ranks 11th globally and earns an AAA rating. The company is the only Singapore insurance brand in the ranking. This article summarises Brand Finance's press release. An earlier version of this article described the ranking as a measure of the strongest insurers. Brand Finance's ranking measures brand value and brand strength as the consultancy calculates them, not an insurer's financial strength, claims-paying ability or customer service, so the article now makes that distinction.

What does the ranking mean? Brand valuation estimates how much a brand is worth, for example by assessing the revenue it contributes and the proportion attributable to the brand itself. The method is Brand Finance's own, and different consultancies reach different valuations. Brand strength is a separate measure based on a scorecard, and Brand Finance says Great Eastern's 81.4 places it eleventh worldwide. The press release does not name the other brands at the top of the list, so we cannot report who leads the ranking.

What drove Great Eastern's performance? According to the release, revenue growth came from stronger new policy sales and better agency performance in Singapore and Malaysia. Brand Finance also credits new product launches and growth in the financial advisor and bancassurance channels in Singapore. Bancassurance means selling insurance through bank branches and channels. These are the consultancy's explanations, and the release does not provide the underlying financial figures, so readers who want to assess the company's results should look at Great Eastern's own reports.

How did the sector do? The top 100 insurance brands grew 14% year on year to a combined US$606.7 billion, which Brand Finance describes as the sector's largest brand-value increase in five years. Great Eastern's 2% growth was therefore below the sector's rate, which is why its value rank of 33rd should be read alongside its strong brand-strength score. In other words, the brand is highly rated on quality measures but did not grow as fast in value terms as the average of the top 100.

What is the outlook? Brand Finance expects growth to moderate as rate-driven tailwinds fade. In the insurance context, rate-driven tailwinds refers to higher premiums and investment yields that boosted results in recent years. The consultancy expects insurers that invest in trust, digital capability, underwriting quality and long-term value creation to be best placed to keep growing. Alex Haigh, Managing Director of Brand Finance Asia Pacific, said that an insurance brand's success is not determined by scale alone. That comment fits with Great Eastern's position: it ranks higher on strength than on value.

Why do brand rankings matter to customers? A strong brand can signal that a company is well known and trusted, but it should not be the only basis for choosing an insurer. Customers should look at financial strength ratings from agencies, claims-handling records, product features and prices. The Monetary Authority of Singapore regulates insurers and publishes information on the sector, and the Life Insurance Association Singapore publishes industry data. Brand Finance's ranking is a commercial product, and companies featured in it sometimes publicise their ranking, as Great Eastern's release suggests.

What are the limitations? The ranking depends on public financial information and on the consultancy's estimates and survey data. It does not include every insurer, and it measures the brand, not the entire company. For Great Eastern, the figure of US$4.9 billion is a notional value of the brand and not the value of the company or its shares.

How should readers interpret a brand-strength rating of AAA? Brand Finance's press release gives the score of 81.4 and the AAA rating, without setting out the full scale. The score reflects factors such as marketing investment, stakeholder equity and business performance as the consultancy measures them, according to its general description of the method. It indicates that a brand is well regarded and valuable, and that is useful to the company in attracting agents, partners and customers. It is not a rating of the insurer's ability to pay claims, which agencies such as AM Best, S&P and Fitch assess separately.

What about Malaysia? The release mentions better agency performance in both Singapore and Malaysia, which reflects the fact that Great Eastern operates in both markets. The release does not give figures for each country, so we cannot say how much each contributed. Readers wanting detail should consult the company's own financial reports.

For the wider sector, the 14% rise in value suggests that insurance brands benefited from strong results and from market conditions. Whether that continues depends on interest rates, claims and competition, which Brand Finance itself says are likely to moderate growth. This article summarises a press release and does not endorse any company. It is not investment advice.
image_alt: Singapore insurance brand strength and the city-state's financial hub (illustrative)
key_points: Great Eastern's brand value is US$4.9 billion, up 2% year on year, ranking 33rd among the world's top 100 insurance brands; it is the only Singapore insurance brand in the ranking.
Its Brand Strength Index score is 81.4 out of 100, ranking 11th globally, with an AAA brand strength rating.

Brand Finance credits revenue growth from stronger new policy sales and better agency performance in Singapore and Malaysia, plus new products and growth in financial advisor and bancassurance channels in Singapore.
The top 100 insurance brands grew 14% to a combined US$606.7 billion, the largest sector brand-value increase in five years.
Brand Finance expects growth to moderate as rate-driven tailwinds fade, favouring insurers that invest in trust, digital capability, underwriting quality and long-term value.
why_it_matters: Brand value is a commercial estimate, not a measure of financial strength, but a strong brand helps an insurer keep customers and sell new products. The ranking also shows how much value the insurance sector gained in a year.
